transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Iran says it is ready for any renewed war waged by the U.S. and Israel.
NPR's Hadil Al-Shalji reports.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Arakchi told Iranian state media
that just as his country is prepared for diplomacy, it's prepared for war.
Arakchi said that "any scenario is conceivable, including the possibility
of an attack by the U.S. and Israel."
The U.S. and Israel are preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran in early November,
according to a person briefed on the matter speaking to NPR in the condition of anonymity.
Iranian state media also quoted a security source saying that if Iranian officials or
civilian infrastructure were attacked, Iran would retaliate by targeting U.S.
interests in the region, as well as the infrastructure and assets of countries participating in the war.
Hadil Al-Shalji, NPR News, Istanbul.
The pro-Israel political organization, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee,
has made an announcement. The group, also known as APAC, says it will no longer issue endorsements,
make direct PAC contributions, or earmark funds for candidates, NPR's Sage Miller reports.
APAC started its political involvement five years ago, but the pro-Israel group has caught
a lot of heat this election cycle over its stances on various issues, such as the war in Gaza.
APAC has also become a liability for some candidates endorsed by the group.
They've come under fire on both the right and the left for accepting APAC support and money.
But APAC isn't going away.
In a letter to members, the group says its super PAC, United Democracy Project, will stick around.
The super PAC will be able to raise an unlimited amount of money and has spent
heavily to support pro-Israel candidates and oppose those who criticize Israel.
Sage Miller, NPR News.
Vice President Vance campaigned yesterday in Ohio from member station WVXU.
Tana Weingartner reports Vance has weighed in on a controversial campaign ad in the Ohio race for governor.
An attack ad from Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign features the estranged mother of
Democratic candidate Amy Acton, accusing her of lying about several parts of her childhood,
including a sexual assault. The vice president said politics is a tough business
and Republicans should focus on winning rather than choosing a side about a commercial.
Well, I'll be honest with you, whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern.
What is my concern is who's going to govern the next generation of American government.
Court records show Dr. Amy Acton's stepfather was charged with sexually assaulting Acton when she
was 12 but never stood trial. Acton says she hasn't spoken with her mother in nearly 50 years.
For NPR News, I'm Tana Weingartner in Cincinnati.
You're listening to NPR News.
Heavy storms are still streaming through Arizona. There are a couple of severe thunderstorm
warnings east and northeast of Phoenix. Severe weather also hit the state yesterday. The National
Weather Service says hail sometimes. The size of golf balls hammered several areas in Arizona.
There are reports of damaged roofs, dented cars and windows that shattered.
New Mexico's Democratic Attorney General announced a civil lawsuit against associates
of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. NPR's Ava Berger reports.
New Mexico's Attorney General, Raul Torres, named Epstein's long-time attorney Darren Indike and his
accountant Richard Cahn in the lawsuit. Both are co-executors of Epstein's estate and the lawsuit
alleges that the two men helped facilitate, finance and conceal Epstein's sex trafficking operation.
We are here today to mark an important milestone and the use of another legal tool at our disposal
to hopefully shed light on individuals in Jeffrey Epstein's orbit.
The civil lawsuit asked the court to prevent the two men from profiting potentially tens of
millions of dollars from the estate. Lawyers for the men reject the allegations and deny that they
in any way knowingly facilitated Epstein's sexual abuse or trafficking. Ava Berger, NPR News.
The Vatican says Pope Leo's doctors have determined he does not need more medical treatment.
Surgeons removed part of his lung last week to treat cancer. I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News.

topics.text: Iran says it is ready for war as U.S. and Israel reportedly plan possible attack
AIPAC announces it will stop endorsements and direct PAC contributions, but super PAC continues
Vance weighs in on Ohio governor race attack ad involving Amy Acton's estranged mother
Severe storms with hail hit Arizona, damaging roofs, cars, and windows near Phoenix
New Mexico attorney general sues Jeffrey Epstein's associates over alleged trafficking facilitation
Vatican says Pope Leo needs no further medical treatment after lung surgery for cancer
